opus-5.5.text:
I think the core of it is that synthetic data lets you choose what the model learns from, instead of hoping the right signal is buried in a scrape of the internet. Internet text is a strange distribution. It's full of finished answers but very little of the messy reasoning that produced them. You see the proof, not the hours of failed attempts, the backtracking, the "wait, that's wrong." Synthetic data can fill that gap. You can have models produce long chains of reasoning, check which ones reach correct answers, and train on those.

That leads to what I think matters most: verification. Synthetic data is only as good as your ability to tell good samples from bad ones. In domains like math and code, you have strong verifiers. Unit tests pass or fail, and an answer is right or wrong. So you can generate a huge number of attempts, filter hard, and get a signal that's cleaner than almost anything humans would label by hand. Effectively you're converting compute into data, and that's a very different scaling regime from waiting for more people to write things online.

There's also a targeting benefit. If you notice the model is weak at a particular skill, like long-horizon planning or a certain type of debugging, you can generate data aimed at exactly that weakness. That's much more efficient than hoping more pretraining data happens to cover it.

The obvious worry is model collapse: if you train a model on its own outputs, does it drift into a narrow, degenerate distribution? I think that's a real risk when you naively train on unfiltered generations. But when there's an external grounding signal, like a test suite, a proof checker, or the outcome of a task in an environment, you aren't just recycling the model's beliefs. You're feeding in information about the world that the model didn't have before. That's the distinction that matters. Synthetic data with real verification is closer to a model learning from experience than to a model talking to itself.

So the honest answer is that synthetic data isn't magic on its own. The value comes from pairing generation with a reliable way to check the results. The more domains where we can build good verifiers, the further this approach can go.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the thing to understand is that the real bottleneck for these models isn't compute anymore, it's high-quality tokens. We've basically consumed the internet. And the internet is this weirdly uneven distribution of information. There's an enormous amount about some topics and almost nothing about others, and critically, it almost never shows you the process. You see the final proof, the final code, the final essay. You don't see the person struggling through it, trying three things that didn't work, and then arriving at the answer.

Synthetic data lets you fill in exactly those gaps. You can have a model generate the reasoning traces, the intermediate steps, the failed attempts, and then you can verify whether it got to the right place. That verification piece is the key. In domains like math and code, you have a ground truth signal. The proof checks or it doesn't. The tests pass or they don't. So you can generate a huge amount of data, filter it down to the stuff that's actually correct, and train on that. You're effectively converting compute into tokens, which is a trade we're very happy to make.

The other thing I'd say is that it changes the shape of what the model learns. When you train on filtered synthetic reasoning, you're not just teaching it facts, you're teaching it how to think about a class of problems. And that transfers in ways that are sometimes surprising. We've seen improvements in math reasoning show up as improvements in things that don't look like math at all.

The obvious worry is model collapse, where you train on your own outputs and the distribution degrades. I think that worry is mostly a worry about doing it naively. If you have a strong verifier, or you're using the model to explore a space and keeping only the trajectories that actually work, you're adding information rather than just recycling it. The model is acting as a search process, and the verifier is the thing that makes the search meaningful. That's really the loop that's driving a lot of the progress right now.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is that generating an answer and checking an answer can be very different in difficulty. If a model tries a programming problem a hundred times, and you can run tests to identify which solutions work, you can train on those successful attempts. You’re turning additional computation into better training examples.

But the value isn’t simply that the data is synthetic. If you just sample from a model and train it on everything it produces, you shouldn’t expect automatic improvement. You need some way of selecting, verifying, or improving those outputs. Otherwise, you risk reinforcing the same mistakes.

The other advantage is that you can target the data. If the model struggles with a particular kind of problem, you can generate more examples at the right level of difficulty, rather than hoping those examples happen to exist on the internet. So the exciting thing is the feedback loop: identify a weakness, generate useful practice, check the results, and train again.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is that generating a good answer and recognizing a good answer are different problems. A model might only solve a problem one time in a hundred, but if you can reliably identify that successful attempt, you can train on it. You’re taking something the model can do occasionally and making it something it can do consistently.

Code is a particularly clear example, because you can run it and check whether it passes the tests. That gives you a signal beyond whether the answer looks plausible. And you can generate more problems around the things the model struggles with, so the data is targeted to what it needs to learn.

The caveat is that just producing more text doesn’t necessarily help. If you can’t distinguish good outputs from bad ones, you can reinforce the same mistakes. So a lot of the value comes from the verification and selection process, rather than from the fact that the data is synthetic.
